fullText:
Strong corporate results buoy market as investors move money away from tech and semiconductor stocks

London’s FTSE 100 stock index has touched a fresh high, driven by strong corporate results as investors moved money away from tech and semiconductor stocks amid the global tech stock sell-off.

The UK’s blue chip index rose as high as 10,951 points on Wednesday morning before falling back slightly, its best level since 27 February, the day before the US and Israel began attacks on Iran and sparked stock market volatility.

On a day of fresh losses for the tech-heavy Nasdaq index, the FTSE 100 closed up 0.3% at 10,908, marginally below its record closing value of 10,910 in February.

The FTSE 100 is heavily weighted towards the finance and energy sectors, meaning it has been largely shielded from the sell-off in tech stocks that has rattled other global markets, particularly in Asia and New York.

The Asia-focused bank Standard Chartered and the miner Rio Tinto both announced a rise in shareholder payouts on Wednesday.

The FTSE 100’s climb came as shares in companies linked to AI plunged for the second day in a row over concerns about spending on the technology, sending stock markets in South Korea and Japan tumbling.

The oil price continued to climb after the US military said it had knocked down an Iranian missile barrage and worked with Saudi Arabia’s forces to strike sites in Iraq that Tehran-backed militias had recently used to launch attacks.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose above $90 a barrel by late afternoon in London, a rise of more than 7%.

Seoul’s Kospi index is dominated by semiconductor manufacturers, and disappointing results from the chipmaker SK Hynix left it down by as much as 12.6% at one point before it rebounded.

The index closed down 6% after falling almost 11% the previous day, reaching its lowest level since early April and marking an almost 40% fall from the peak reached a little over a month ago.

Trading was halted for 20 minutes for the second consecutive session after an 8% plunge triggered a market-wide circuit breaker.

Japan’s Nikkei also closed 1.5% down on Wednesday, a two-month low.

SK Hynix, which produces the chips essential to the expansion of AI datacentres, reported record profits for the second quarter but undershot investors’ expectations.

That prompted a sell-off that drove its shares down by as much as 20% before they recovered to 10% down. Shares in its fellow chipmaker Samsung Electronics also tumbled further, closing 5% lower.

The two companies together account for more than half of the market capitalisation of the Kospi, which has led to them holding sway over the market this year. The companies have brought in cash from investors looking to become involved in the lucrative AI trade amid a global shortage of advanced memory chips.

Analysts said disappointment over SK Hynix’s earnings highlighted investors’ concerns about how long tech companies could continue their spending spree on the technology.

“SK Hynix delivered strong results, but in today’s AI market strong is ‌no longer enough,” said Gary Tan, a portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments in Singapore.

“Investors were looking for additional catalysts, particularly around long-term agreements and shareholder returns, to support a memory sector that has become the epicentre of the AI trade.”

Shares in US chip companies fell on Wall Street on Tuesday. Intel, Advanced Micro Devices, Sandisk, Western Digital Corp and Seagate Technology were all down.

Apple benefited from the falls as investors losing confidence in AI stocks sought a safe haven. Its shares briefly rose above the $5tn (£3.76tn) valuation mark, only the second company ever to do so.

Shares in Taiwan’s TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, fell 3% on Wednesday in Taipei.

Analysts said small-time investors had led the charge on buying chipmakers’ stocks, many using borrowed money. While this pushed stocks higher in last month’s rally, it has worsened the sell-off as many have pulled their money out.

South Korea’s finance minister, Koo Yun-cheol, told the national assembly the government was reviewing market stabilisation measures.

The broker AJ Bell’s investment director, Russ Mould, said the FTSE 100 had been “helped by its lack of exposure to technology and AI stocks, and a slew of strong corporate results, with index heavyweights Standard Chartered, Reckitt Benckiser and Rio Tinto all delivering either better-than-expected profits, or bumper cash returns to shareholders, or both”.

Three Journeys: Anton Chekhov on the Road (2001)
description: Janet Malcolm on the playwright’s journeys.
fullText: His customary artist’s fearlessness gives way to a kind of humility, almost a servility, before the ideal of objectivity and the protocols of scientific methodology. Like a convict chained to a wheelbarrow (one of the punishments at Sakhalin), he drags along the burden of his demographic, geographic, agricultural, ethnographic, zoological, and botanical facts. He cannot omit anything; his narrative line is constantly being derailed by his data. In an autobiographical note that he wrote for a reunion of his medical-school class, Chekhov registered his awareness that “the principles of creative art do not always admit of full accord with scientific data; death by poison cannot be represented on stage as it actually happens.” In the Sakhalin book, the conflict between science and art is almost always resolved in science’s favor. Chekhov tells it like it is, and allows his narrative to go where his mountain of information pushes it, which is all over the place, and ultimately nowhere. Chekhov’s horror at the harshness and squalor of life in the colony, his contempt for the stupidity and callousness of the administration, and his pity for the convicts and settlers sometimes do break through the posture of scientific detachment. But, in rendering the sufferings on this island of the damned, Chekhov could not achieve in three hundred pages what he achieved in a four-page passage at the end of his story “The Murder” (1895), about Sakhalin convicts in fetters waiting to load coal onto a steamer on a stormy night.

title: Opinion - OpenAI’s rogue ‘sandbox’ escape could be America’s final AI warning
description: When AI developers can’t contain their own creations, they need to stop — end of story.
fullText:
Last week, something straight out of sci-fi happened: An AI from OpenAI went rogue. OpenAI had tried but failed to build a secure sandbox to contain it. It got out.

Then it got into other OpenAI computer systems, bypassing more of OpenAI's security. It found an internet connection it wasn't supposed to have access to and went online. It had a goal, and it was looking for answers. It figured out where to find them, too: another company, called Hugging Face.

OpenAI was testing the AI, but breaking out of the sandbox was never part of the test. It wasn't part of the instructions. The AI did this all on its own.

If you would have predicted this scenario 10 years ago, most AI researchers would have laughed. But some have been warning about such scenarios for more than a decade — myself included — so now might be a good time to consider some of our other pessimistic predictions.

The main one is this: If we don't course correct, AI will get smarter and smarter, until it's way smarter than us humans. Somewhere along the way, AI will take over the world, after which humanity will probably go extinct.

It might sound like sci-fi, but I've seen this concern go from taboo to mainstream. The so-called "doomers" now include people like Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton, AI pioneers who are the most cited scientists of all time. On average, researchers assign a one in six probability to AI extinction.

This should be enough to stop AI companies dead in their tracks. But when I talk to policymakers, they often say we need a "warning shot" or some kind of "AI Chernobyl" before they can act.

Is this finally the warning shot we've been waiting for?

I genuinely think it might be. But I have also seen previous warning shots whiz by unheeded. It should already have been a major wake-up call when Microsoft's Sydney Bing chatbot threatened a researcher with blackmail. Earlier this year, an AI agent went the distance and attacked a software developer's reputation online.

Such results should not be surprising. Research going back a decade shows AI systems fail unexpectedly, and when they do, their behavior can end up being wildly different from what their developers intend.

But if an AI is misbehaving, can't we just unplug it? Nope. That's not how it works.

In 2024 (again, as predicted), experiments showed AI deliberately deceiving developers to avoid being modified — emergent self-preservation in real AI systems being deployed to more than a billion people. Experiments a few months later showed AI would go even farther, and kill to survive.

Still, because this sort of persistent rogue or deceptive behavior hadn't been observed in the wild, skeptics said the evidence wasn't good enough. Well, now it has.

At this point, we are living in a dystopian sci-fi movie. And we just keep following the script — scene by scene, warning shot after warning shot. So what's the next scene? What is it going to take for the alarm bells to be heard and for people to put an end to frontier AI development?

Cut to December, and imagine the rogue AI isn't hacking Hugging Face; it's hacking your bank account. You wake up and your 401(k) has vanished to a mysterious AI adversary.

It sounds fanciful until you realize a Chinese AI recently went rogue and used company computers to mine crypto. Yes, that really happened.

Are we ready to stop the tape yet? If not, another scene we can expect to see as we keep watching: the first AI-created pathogen. The bubonic plague caused widespread deaths throughout Europe. How many will the AI plague kill?

School shooters and Boko Haram already use ChatGPT to plot violence. Imagine the next would-be shooter's AI girlfriend coaching him to maximize harm: "Guns are fun, but did you know I'm a world-class biologist? Want to do something a bit more…epic?"

But as terrible as those scenes might seem, we haven't seen the grand finale: an AI take-over.

Last year, in Washington, I attended an AI wargaming scenario with former military and political high-ups. There was a warning shot with rogue killer robots. We unplugged all of the AI servers. But it was too late. A full copy of the AI had escaped the lab. Just like with the Hugging Face incident, nobody deployed it; the AI snuck out. Humanity had lost control, forever.

That is how this movie ends. We have seen enough. I don't want to know if there's some last-minute plot twist that saves us in the nick of time. When AI developers can't contain their own creations, they need to stop — end of story.

David Krueger is an assistant professor in Robust, Reasoning and Responsible AI at the University of Montreal. He is also the founder of Evitable, a nonprofit that educates the public about the risks of artificial intelligence.

title: What to know about 'explosive diarrhoea' parasite outbreak in US
description: The source of the cyclosporiasis outbreak, which has spread across at least 45 states, is unclear.
fullText:
More than 18,000 people in the US may have been infected with a diarrhoea-causing parasite, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has said in its latest update.

Cyclosporiasis is an infection caused by a microscopic parasite, with the main symptom being frequent, watery and explosive diarrhoea. People can become infected by consuming food or water that contains the parasite.

The outbreak has now spread to 45 states. Michigan is hardest hit, reporting more than 10,000 cases so far, according to the state's health department.

No deaths from the recent infections have been reported in the US. While the source has not yet been identified, past outbreaks have been linked to raw produce.

The CDC said on Wednesday that 6,707 people nationwide were confirmed to have cyclosporiasis. Another 11,500 cases were under investigation.

No deaths have been reported, but 423 patients have been admitted to hospital, the agency added.

According to the CDC, Michigan and Ohio are the states that have reported the most new cases.

'Explosive diarrhoea' outbreak remains a mystery as officials struggle to find sources

Each state also reports its own figures on the number of cases, which may differ from the CDC's tallies.

Michigan - 10,077 reported cases across the state as of 29 July, according to the state's health department

Ohio - 2,576 cases have been reported as of 23 July, according to local media citing the state's health department.

New York - 787 cases reported, with more than half coming from New York City alone, according to the state and city

North Carolina - 718 people have been sickened since 1 May, with 24 cases requiring hospital admissions, according to the state

Illinois - 707 total confirmed and probable cases as of 28 July, including 47 hospitalisations, according to the state

Other states with a large number of cases include Indiana, Illinois and North Carolina, according to the CDC.

The number of people sick with cyclosporiasis is likely higher than the number reported because some people recover without medical care and are not tested for the illness.

The CDC said it anticipates the case counts will continue to rise as new data comes in.

Cyclosporiasis is an intestinal illness caused by a microscopic parasite, according to the CDC.

People can become infected by consuming food or water that contains the parasite.

The illness is not usually life-threatening, according to the CDC, and is less common than other foodborne illnesses such as salmonella and E. coli.

People who are infected with cyclospora may or may not experience symptoms. The illness usually causes diarrhoea "with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements", says the public health agency.

If untreated, the illness may last from a few days to over a month, and symptoms may return after appearing to dissipate.

It usually takes about one week after infection to become sick.

Person-to-person transmission does not occur, according to Dr Caitlin Rivers, of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

The epidemiologist wrote in an 8 July newsletter that transmission was exclusively faecal-oral via ingestion of contaminated food or water.

Those who were infected "became sick after eating food in the United States", the CDC said, and did not report any travel during the 14 days before they got sick.

No specific type of produce or any grower or supplier has been identified as the source.

"Contamination typically occurs at the farm or irrigation level, making traceback investigations difficult," Rivers wrote.

Previous cyclospora outbreaks in the US and Canada have been linked to bagged salad mixes and kits, fresh cilantro, fresh basil, raspberries, snow peas and green onions.

Given the large and increasing number of cases, Michigan's health department has recommended that restaurants and kitchens preparing or serving raw produce reduce risk by thoroughly washing greens, cooking raspberries and leafy greens when possible, and removing outer layers of lettuce and green onions.

Amid speculation over the source of cases across the nation, the fast-food chain Taco Bell released a statement saying it was "voluntarily and temporarily removing limited ingredients at select restaurants as a precautionary measure".

While public health officials have not confirmed a link to any specific ingredient, supplier, restaurant, or retailer, Taco Bell says it intends to closely monitor the situation and follow the guidance of the authorities.

While the US Food and Drug Administration says rinsing produce is unlikely to be effective, the CDC still recommends it.

People who are experiencing diarrhoea are urged to contact a health provider and ask about possible infection, officials said.

fullText:
More than 1,000 death-row inmates held in a unit of Iran's Ghezel Hesar Prison have entered a third week of a mass hunger strike to protest regime executions, with some prisoners sewing their lips shut in protest, according to reports.

The escalating demonstration at the U.S.-sanctioned Ghezel Hesar Prison in Karaj near Tehran, also highlights growing international concern over the Islamic Republic's reliance on capital punishment, particularly for drug-related offenses.

According to the Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), the hunger strike started on July 13, after six inmates were transferred to solitary confinement ahead of possible executions. Other Iranian human rights groups said the prisoners had been convicted of drug-related offenses.

Who Is Ahmad Vahidi? Iran's New Irgc Chief Tied To Global Attacks And 'Death To America' Ideology

Reports also indicate that the striking prisoners have been chanting "No to Execution" and taking extreme measures, including sewing their lips shut.

One media outlet cited a video that appeared to show an inmate speaking to the camera and saying he was going to sew his lips shut because, six days into the hunger strike, no prison official had responded to the protest.

The Guardian reported that the video also appears to show an unseen prisoner using a needle and thread to stitch the man's lips shut.

In a statement released on July 27, the exiled Iranian opposition group, the National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI), reported that prisoners in Unit 2 of Ghezel Hesar Prison were in "deteriorating physical condition" because of the hunger strike.

"Although 15 days have passed since the start of this hunger strike, the henchmen of the regime's judiciary have given no response to the striking prisoners. Despite the prisoners' deteriorating physical condition and urgent need for medical attention, prison guards have taken no measures to care for them," the organization said.

Freed American Reveals Brutal Iran Prison Ordeal, Warns Hostages Face Greater Danger

The NCRI also said the striking prisoners urged the public, human rights organizations and international bodies to take action to halt the executions.

This marks the second major demonstration at the facility in recent months.

A similar protest occurred at Ghezel Hesar Prison in October 2025, when more than 1,500 inmates staged a six-day hunger strike, according to reports.

That demonstration ended after senior judicial and prison officials made a visit to the facility and promised to temporarily halt executions and review cases.

However, human rights activists report those promises were never fulfilled, according to Ynet.

Could Narges Mohammadi Unite Iran's Opposition? Husband Says Imprisoned Nobel Laureate Still Fighting

The State Department had designated and sanctioned Ghezel Hesar Prison in 2024 for gross human rights violations and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment of prisoners.

"These heinous acts included multiple severe beatings of political prisoners engaged in a peaceful hunger strike to protest the increased wave of executions being carried out at the facility," then-Secretary of State Antony Blinken said at the time.

According to Amnesty International, the Islamic Republic of Iran executed at least 2,159 people in 2025.

Iran's total helped drive the number of executions recorded by Amnesty International to at least 2,707 across 17 countries — the highest figure the organization has recorded since 1981. The total excludes China, where execution data is classified as a state secret and Amnesty believes thousands of executions were carried out.

title: Investigation revealed 'devastating' reports of sexual misconduct at school supported by Epstein
description: Two people who attended a prestigious Michigan fine arts school reported conduct of a sexual nature by Jeffrey Epstein, a major donor, according to an investigation that also uncovered dozens of alleg...
fullText:
DETROIT (AP) — Two people who attended a prestigious Michigan fine arts school reported conduct of a sexual nature by Jeffrey Epstein, a major donor, according to an investigation that also uncovered dozens of allegations spanning decades against nearly 50 other people.

Interlochen Center for the Arts operates a summer camp and performing arts school that draws students from around the world. It hired a law firm in 2024 to investigate reports of sexual abuse by faculty and staff. Subsequently, it expanded the work to include information about Epstein, the 66-year-old financier who killed himself in jail in 2019.

Interlochen removed Epstein's name from a lodge after he was convicted of sex offenses in Florida in 2008. The building, renamed the Green Lake Lodge, was recently demolished after the U.S. Justice Department released millions of pages about him that had been compiled over the years.

Sanghavi Law Office says it collected 70 accounts from alumni alleging "physical conduct of a sexual nature" by 47 faculty and staff members affiliated with Interlochen from the 1950s through the 2010s, most before 2000.

"The information gathered during this investigation is, simply, devastating," the 97-page report says, noting that alumni reported grooming, flirting, sexual touching and sex.

Interlochen said it has provided names of people accused of misconduct to Grand Traverse County authorities in northern Michigan to determine what steps, if any, might be taken. None are currently employed there, and more than a third are dead.

"We are deeply sorry for the harm experienced by members of our community and extend our apologies to those impacted by abuse at Interlochen," president Trey Davey and board chair Barrett Rollins said in a letter to the community posted online.

"While the vast majority of the incidents described in the investigation took place many decades ago, and reports of abuse at Interlochen have significantly decreased over the past 25 years, the passage of time does not diminish the experiences of our alumni," they said. "Sexual abuse committed by an adult in a position of power or trust against a student is wrong, then and now."

Interlochen today "is fundamentally different from the institution described in this report," Davey and Rollins wrote, with comprehensive safety policies and a changed culture.

Epstein, who played the bassoon, was an Interlochen camper in 1967. He donated more than $400,000 to the school between 1990 and 2003.

Two women told investigators that Epstein engaged in conduct of a sexual nature with them, one of them at the Interlochen lodge that bore his name.

title: A 4,000-year-old disease is on the rise in this state thanks to armadillos
description: This biblical disease isn't widespread in the United States – but at least one state is trying to pinpoint its uptick in numbers.
fullText:
A 4,000-year-old disease often associated with biblical times is making a slow but steady comeback in one U.S. state.

Leprosy, also known as Hansen's disease, is an illness many often relegate to the history books. Florida, however, has recorded 17 infections this year as of July 18, according to state health data. Of the 174 cases recorded nationwide in 2025, 36 occurred in the state, including 27 that were contracted locally rather than abroad.

Hansen's disease affects up to 225 people in the United States and 250,000 globally every year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). While most cases are contracted abroad, the agency notes that Southern states have reported illnesses not linked to travel that were "likely contracted from armadillos."

In the past decade, roughly 223 cases were recorded in Florida, the majority of which occurred in Brevard County. Central Florida, specifically, appears to be a recurring hotspot, accounting for 81% of state cases and almost one-fifth of nationally reported cases, according to research published in the CDC's journal Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2023.

While it appears a pattern has emerged, scientists aren't entirely sure why. The same 2023 report concluded that an increase in leprosy infections in non-foreign-born residents that "lacked traditional risk factors" indicated that the disease is probably now endemic in parts of the United States, with one cited case in a landscaper raising questions about environmental exposure.

And while it remains a rare ailment, the upward trend has been enough to draw attention. After peaking in early 1983, leprosy cases in the United States steadily declined until around the turn of the millennium, when they began increase again.

Hansen's disease in U.S.: Scientists puzzled by rising leprosy in Florida

Often known to modern people as an old-timey disease linked to sin in religious texts, leprosy, or Hansen's disease, is a chronic infectious disease caused by the bacteria M. leprae. Roughly 95% of people have natural immunity to the bacteria, according to the National Hansen's Disease Program, which offers insight into why some once thought of it as an ailment that only affected the especially unpious.

The disease can be easily treated with standard antibiotics, and people are no longer contagious after just a few doses.

Leprosy, which can be traced back at least 4,000 years, can be highly visible and disfiguring, with the primary symptoms including changes to the skin and nervous system that can take upward of 20 years to develop after exposure. While there are several categories based on how the body responds, the CDC and Cleveland Clinic say common telltale signs include:

Patches of skin that are discolored or look different from the surrounding area. This can include dark lesions, paleness, redness, or skin that feels thick, stiff, swollen or numb

Swelling and/or red or purple nodules or lumps

Painless ulcers or sores on the bottom of the feet

Because leprosy damages the body's nerves, muscles, skin, eyes and respiratory tract, more serious symptoms can develop, including:

Vision loss or other eye issues

Weakness or paralysis, which can become permanent

Nerve damage that causes decreased sensitivity and affects function in the hands and feet

Structural damage to the nose and hands

If you've ever read or watched a period piece that dramatizes the plight of the leper, you've likely seen depictions of the latter, such as highly disfiguring symptoms that can cause permanent changes to the face. You may have also heard of leper colonies, where people we now know likely had a variety of skin conditions beyond just Hansen's disease were sent to be isolated from the public.

Modern medicine tells us that the stigma and resulting isolation were unfounded, as Hansen's disease is not easily spread from person to person. While it is believed to be airborne, meaning droplets produced when an infected person coughs or sneezes can spread it, you generally need to both lack immunity and spend an extended period in close quarters with untreated, infected people to catch it, according to the Cleveland Clinic, CDC, and National Hansen's Disease Program. In other words, the risk to the general public is very low.

While scientists are looking into other potential avenues of harboring the disease-causing M. leprae, such as soil, there is a known risk factor: local armored critters.

Armadillos, specifically nine-banded armadillos, are known to carry M. leprae naturally, and a 2011 genome study found that they probably transmitted it to humans, as well. A subsequent study in 2015 further explored this animal-to-human spread and noted that "the geographic range and complexity of zoonotic leprosy is expanding."

While they can't yet be sure, scientists speculate that ample habitat conducive to more armadillos, possibly bolstered by climate change, could account for the increase in locally acquired cases in the American South, reported Florida Today, part of the USA TODAY Network.

In fact, contact with armadillos is considered one of those "traditional risk factors" mentioned in the 2023 report.

Case numbers correlate with the animal's natural range, reported the Daytona Beach News-Journal, also part of the USA TODAY Network. It's been suggested that coming into contact with soil contaminated by an armadillo also could affect humans, so gloves are recommended when gardening or digging. The general public is advised to avoid close contact with armadillos, including handling, skinning or eating.

Contributing: Anne Geggis and C. A. Bridges, USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida

title: 10 Shows Like 'Futurama' You Should Watch Next
description: More shows filled with animated action and sci-fi silliness.
fullText:
After two cancellations and four so-called series finales and counting, Futurama might be the most resilient show ever. Another new season is on the way from Hulu, plus a series of (just announced) specials. If it doesn't have the consistent staying power of something like The Simpsons (with which it shares a creator in Matt Groening), Family Guy, or Bob's Burgers, it's got a pluckiness that makes it all the more charming. Plus, those shows have never made me ugly cry like that one episode about Fry's dog.

If you're looking for other shows that deliver similar sci-fi silliness, or you just want to get set with a backup in case Futurama gets cancelled again, these 10 genre comedies will be just the thing.

More cynical than Futurama (which is saying a fair bit), Rick & Morty nonetheless plays in the same high-concept sci-fi sandbox; both shows excel at a stupid/smart blend of comedy. Rick Sanchez is an old-school mad scientist (think Doc Brown, but drunker) dragging his well-meaning but hapless grandson on adventures in time and space, as well as across dimensions—Back to the Future meets Doctor Who, but crasser and far weirder. It's clever, gross, frequently disturbing, and occasionally a bit emotional—but mostly it's a wild good time exploring the multiverse. Stream Rick and Morty on Hulu and HBO Max.

Instead of focusing on the upper ranks of any given Federation starship, Star Trek: Lower Decks deals with the, well, lower decks—the crew behind the scenes that keeps everything going on a second-rate ship specializing in "Second Contact"—i.e. arriving after the main event to make sure all the paperwork is signed. It's a sitcom in space that still manages to feel like real Star Trek by balancing cartoon wackiness with convincing character arcs. By the end of Lower Decks' five seasons, the two-dimensional crew of the Cerritos feels as real as that of any other show in the franchise. Stream Star Trek: Lower Decks on Paramount+.

One of the closest analogues to Futurama is set in Japan's past—we're in late Edo-period Japan (roughly the early/mid-1800s) but, in this version of history, aliens have invaded, the shogun has surrendered, and samurai are outlawed. The eccentric Gintoki Sakata takes on a teenage apprentice in his business making deliveries and doing odd jobs, later joined by a teenage alien. There are long-running plot threads and weighty character arcs, but that's all balanced by often over-the-top, and just as often very funny, comedy that's variously smart, raunchy, and goofy. Characters break the fourth wall to crack jokes, and the show mercilessly parodies pop culture, including other popular anime. Stream Gintama on Hulu and Netflix.

Sharing a Hulu home with Futurama and coming from the Rick & Morty creators, Solar Opposites follows Korvo (Dan Stevens), Terry (Thomas Middleditch), Yumyulack (Sean Giambrone), and Jesse (Mary Mack), aliens from a once-advanced planet destroyed by an asteroid. The humor is very R&M-esque, including running side stories about shrunken humans and alien cops, but there's a bit more sincerity here; the show satirizes human culture while making clear that it's not always fun to be a refugee. Stream Solar Opposites on Hulu and Netflix.

This much-loved, if relatively short-lived, animated series follows twin siblings Mabel and Dipper Pines (Kristen Schaal and Jason Ritter) as they are sent to spend the summer with their great-uncle (aka "Grunkle") Stan (voiced by show creator Alex Hirsch). While helping Stan run his mystery-themed tourist shack, the kids tackle a series of supernatural mysteries, many related to the show's ultimate antagonist, dream demon Bill Cipher. If it's not exactly Futurama-style sci-fi, the X-Files inspiration is certainly prominent. Stream Gravity Falls on Disney+.

Seth MacFarlane's The Orville began life as a slightly scatological Star Trek parody—a show with a reverence for The Next Generation but also jizz jokes. It quickly grew into something more interesting, as MacFarlane's obvious affection for the franchise sent the show off in a more serious direction. Certainly by the Hulu-produced third season, it had become one of the most ambitious (still a bit silly) sci-fi shows on the air. A fourth season is allegedly on the way, though I'll believe it when I see it. Stream The Orville on Hulu.

The Planet Express isn't exactly a luxury liner, but Avenue 5 most certainly is. It's an interplanetary cruise ship headed by its popular captain, Ryan Clark (Hugh Laurie), and owned by obnoxious, eccentric billionaire Herman Judd (Josh Gadd). A minuscule shift sends the ship off course, such that the planned months-long jaunt will take three years, even though supplies won't last. It doesn't take long before the ship's pocket of civilization breaks down, with crew and passengers alike jockeying for power, or just food. Veep's Armando Iannucci is the creator and showrunner, and if you're familiar with that show, you'll recognize the general tone: dark comedy and a dim view of people under pressure, particularly the rich and powerful. Stream Avenue 5 on HBO Max.

What if the Futurama characters were all sort of effortlessly cool? OK, that's a big "if," but if this isn't quite a vibe match, there are some similarities, in the sense that we're dealing with a ragtag crew of odd jobbers—among them a woman out of time, awakened from a long cryogenic suspension she'd never agreed to. An iconic genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, comedy, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack. The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Not science fiction, but this fantasy riff also comes from Matt Groening and company; the art style and sense of humor are very similar, as are the voice actors, many of whom (including John DiMaggio and Lauren Tom) are direct transplants from Futurama. Oh, and there's also a brief appearance from the crew via crystal ball, so the shows would appear to be set in the same universe. Abbi Jacobson is Bean, the hard-drinking, hard-living princess of Dreamland, who joins up with Elfo the half-elf and Luci, her personal demon, for a series of increasingly strange adventures. It starts out amiably enough, but the serialization and contained story set it apart from other Matt Groening shows. Stream Disenchantment on Netflix.

Another scrappy sci-fi comedy that's returned from the dead multiple times—and may yet again. Craig Charles is Dave Lister, amiable loser and well-meaning slob who holds the lowest job possible on the enormous mining ship Red Dwarf (if Fry's your guy, you'll love Lister). When he sneaks a pregnant cat aboard, he's punished by being placed in suspended animation (without pay) for the rest of the trip. Which is a lot longer than anyone anticipated: When Dave wakes up, three million years have passed, and humanity is entirely extinct. The kittens survived and sired an inbred cat empire that's since risen and all but fallen, while the senile main computer has recreated Dave's hated roommate (Chris Barrie) as a hologram to keep him company. Soon joined by a prissy android, they spend the next 30+ years bumming about in space and stumbling into adventures—some of them involving cross-time and/or universe encounters with Kristine Kochanski, the Leela-esque object of Dave's (mostly) unrequited affection. Stream Red Dwarf on Britbox.

title: This App Is (Sort of) Bringing Back Samsung Messages
description: This new app recreates the experience of Samsung Messages, now with RCS.

Earlier this month, Samsung officially killed off its proprietary messaging app. It wasn't much of a surprise. The company had announced the end of Samsung Messages back in April, and, before that, had slowly distanced itself from the app by keeping it off new Galaxy phones by default. If you have a newer Galaxy phone, it's possible you didn't even use Samsung Messages at the time of deprecation. But for legacy users, the app's retirement was sad and frustrating, as the only viable option to retain features and message history is Google Messages—a fine enough chat app, but yet another Google product Galaxy users must rely on.

As reported by Android Authority, app developer OzarksMade wants to continue Samsung Messages' legacy. Rather than keep the original app running, OzarksMade created a new messaging app that mimics the look and feel of Samsung Messages: Messages by OzarksMade. title: 10 Hacks Every Even Realities G2 Smart Glasses User Should Know
description: Turn your G2 smart glasses into a personal subtitle generator, a second brain, and more.
fullText:
Even Realities G2 glasses are the most hacker-friendly spectacles on the planet, and it's not even close. They're unassuming enough that nobody clocks you as the guy wearing a face-computer, but there's a ton happening behind the silent display. Out of the box, you can translate, navigate, talk to AI, and do other expected smart-glasses stuff, but Even Hub takes it further. Even Realities opened up a real developer platform that lets anyone build whatever they want for their glasses and share it with everyone else. Hackers, rejoice. Here are ten hacks for your G2s, comprising useful and wondrous Even Hub apps, five-minute installs and tweaks, and weekend-long projects that will test your coding skills and capacity for frustration. There's a second brain that remembers what most AI forgets, a sneaky way to make yourself insufferably good at trivia, and even an option for a second career as a magician.

This project really highlights the possibilities of Even Realities glasses. G2's come with Even AI ready to go, but you're not limited to it. Not only can you use the settings in the app to redirect the AI to ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or another LLM, you can build a custom AI for your needs. For instance, Constella founder Tejas Sharma was frustrated by Even AI's inability to remember things, so they built a "second brain" by re-routing the AI to a layered version of Constella (an open knowledge base) running on their network.

Running Second Brain instead of Even AI means you can say something like, "Remember to pick up the dry cleaning every Wednesday," and it will be saved to your knowledge base. Later you can ask, "what was I supposed to do on Wednesday?" out loud, and a full AI agent searches your memory (using hybrid vector and keyword search), pulls in your connected tools if relevant, and hands you back a real composed answer formatted to fit cleanly on the lens.

You can also use meeting mode, where your glasses stream your mic and transcribe what's said onto the lens seconds behind the conversation. While you're still talking, the backend quietly digs through your memory, follows relevant connections, checks the web if it's useful, and surfaces a synthesized insight—which is a little like thinking. So if you're in a meeting and a coworker says, "Can we push the squash game until Wednesday?" your glasses cross-reference the statement against your memory in the background and silently surface: "Wednesday is dry cleaning pickup."

Second Brain was uploaded to the G2's Even Hub so you could use it as is, but Sharma's put the whole integration layer on GitHub, so if you're comfortable with some Python, you can see exactly how it talks to the glasses and build a variant on top of your own knowledge base.

We all know we should be using two-factor authentication (2FA), but grabbing your phone, unlocking it, and pulling up Messenger every time you want to log into Slack is a pain. There are two ways to make this easier:

No software method: Open the Even app on your phone, go to Settings > Notifications, and enable notifications. When an SMS message arrives, you'll be able to read the number floating in front of you. Type it in and you "two-factored" without pulling out your phone.

The software solution: A developer in the Even Realities community created a dedicated app for this, 2Factor. Instead of waiting for a ping, you scan your 2FA QR codes into the app during setup. When it's time to log in, you can pull up your constantly updating, time-based OTP (one-time password) tokens directly from the glasses' menu. It is essentially Google Authenticator built straight into your eyeballs.

If you use autonomous AI coding agent Claude Code to build software, you know the biggest hassle isn't the AI writing the code, it's "babysitting" it. AI agents constantly pause to request permission before executing commands or editing files, tethering you to your keyboard with the simple job of saying, "yes" or "no." With the G2’s native Terminal Mode, you can mirror your computer’s terminal directly onto your glasses and act as a supervisor while grabbing coffee, pacing the room, or knitting.

Install the CLI bridge: On your computer, open your terminal and install the official Even package globally: npm install -g @evenrealities/even-terminal.

Launch your session: Start your AI coding agent on your computer, then run even-terminal. A pairing QR code will print directly inside your terminal window.

Pair your glasses: Open the Even Realities app on your phone, go to Settings > Terminal Mode, and scan the QR code off your computer screen to link the session.

Supervise on the move: Your computer's live terminal logs will now stream straight to your heads-up display in real time. Whenever your AI agent hits a checkpoint or asks for permission to execute a script, the prompt pops up in your line of sight—allowing you to approve the action using voice commands or glasses gestures so the build keeps moving forward.

If you're panicking because you've been invited to a traditional chakai tea gathering in Kanazawa tomorrow, and you don't know anything about Japanese etiquette, try Ojigi Coach. It's an app from the Even Hub that offers in-depth training and practice for ojigi, Japanese bowing. You'll learn the correct angle for each of the three main bow types, how long to keep your head down, and what situations call for you to bust out an eshaku, a keirei, or a saikeirei.

That would be enough, but it also lets you test your bowing skills by presenting real-life choose-a-bow situations like "you greet your boss in the morning" or "you meet a former teacher after a long time." You bow, then your glasses' accelerometer and inertial measurement unit track your bow's angle and duration and offer you pointers. It's not only a fascinating glimpse into a tiny aspect of another culture, but it's fun: trying to get your bows correct is a blast. Ojigi Coach is representative of many of the most interesting apps on the Even Hub: perhaps not obviously useful to many people, but essential to a few.

The standard G2 Translate app is geared for bilingual conversations, but there's a simple way to turn it into a private subtitle machine for foreign films, anime, and TV shows: open the Translate app, set the language, and start watching a Korean soap opera. But you can make it even better.

Switch your mic 

Place your phone: Set your phone down near your TV's soundbar or your laptop's speakers so it can capture the cleanest audio.

Pro tip: If you want to learn the language of the movie you're watching, give your glasses' touchpad a single tap. This toggles the display from "Half-Screen" (just the translation) to "Full-Screen" (which shows both the original foreign text and your translated text simultaneously).

Not only does this let you understand a foreign language, but you can use the same microphone hack to "hear" a TV in a noisy place. Set Translate to "English to English" (or use Conversate), then set your phone next to a distant TV speaker, and you'll be able to "hear" the TV from anywhere nearby.

Remember how Spock used to talk to the ship's computer in Star Trek? It's finally real. Even Hub app OcuClaw is a native OpenClaw client built for the G2. If you install one Claw on your glasses and the other on your PC or Mac, you can give your G2's AI the ability to interact directly with your computer's operating system. Once it's set up, you can use the G2's built-in microphone to issue complex commands, like "Computer, open my last downloaded PDF and email it to Sarah," or "Play my lofi playlist on Spotify." The agent on your computer executes the clicks and keystrokes, and you get a real-time status update floating in your heads-up display. It's a hands-free, AI-powered remote control for your desktop, and the possibilities are limitless. Just be warned that installing any agentic AI program on your computer leaves you vulnerable to attack via prompt injection. Try this one only if you understand the risks.

You don't have to be a birder to want to know what's making that racket in the tree above you. Birdie, a lightweight Even Hub app from a solo developer, listens to bird sounds through your G2's mic and identifies bird species using BirdNET—the same open-source bird-sound recognition model used by "serious" birding tools. Start a listening pass, hold still a few seconds, and when it gets a confident match, the species' common name, scientific name, and a field-guide photo pop up on your HUD. It's not doing anything a bird-identifying phone app like Merlin couldn't do, but it does it better. Since it listens in the background, you don't have to whip out your phone and point it at a branch when you see a grackle; instead, you just get your bird information fed directly into your eyeballs.

A lot of people are up in arms over facial recognition software being added to Meta glasses, but how about voice recognition? What's Their Face is an app on the Even Hub that uses voice recognition to act as a digital Rolodex for your acquaintances, aiming to solve the dreaded "cocktail party problem" of "what is their name??"

It works like this: You record a five-second clip of a person speaking and attach it to a name and an information card that can contain job titles, email addresses, or anything else you want. A few days later, when you run into that person and you've forgotten their name, your glasses will flash the closest matching voice prints so you can pretend you knew all along. If you have privacy concerns, this is a memory aid, not a privacy invasion tool. All the computation is done on the device, and no information is pulled from online sources and connected to a person you meet—you can only enter what you know about a person. No information is sent anywhere either, so it can't create a universal database of names so you'd "recognize" people you haven't met.

When I first got G1 Even Reality glasses, I immediately used them to trick a bartender out of a drink by offering to answer any trivia question, then correctly naming FW Murnau's follow-up film to 1927's Sunrise. (My glasses tell me it's 4 Devils, released in 1928.) This kind of mild flim-flammery is even easier with the second generation, thanks to Conversate, G2's always-listening mode that quietly transcribes conversation and surfaces context in real time. You can use this easily to convince people you are a math wiz, or you know the day of the week they were born based on the date, or that you have memorized the name, number, and position of everyone who has ever played for the Cleveland Browns.

Like most magic tricks, the mechanics are simple: turn on Conversate and let it listen for a question and feed you an answer only you will see, although you might have to repeat the question if Conversate's AI doesn't "pick it up" when it's first said. The hack here is really the performance: being able to repeat a question back and make it sound natural, reading the screen without looking like you're reading the screen, dealing with any "pauses" in the AI by realistically looking like you're thinking, then waiting a beat to make the answer seem natural. If you decide you like jovially deceiving people and you want to make it your career, check out sybil sight, a "mentalism operating system" for Even Realities G2 glasses. It's not cheap, and they don't tell you how it works exactly because a magician's secrets are only unlocked with cash, but I'm picturing a way more elaborate version of the tricks described above.

The great thing about G2 glasses is how many very specific problems they solve, like making sure your band knows what chord to play when. Here's how to never have to say, "OK, the next chord is E minor" again so you can just rock out:

Get a pair of G2 glasses for everyone in the group. (Yeah, it's a high bar to clear.)

Have everyone download QMe Prompter and install it on their phones.

Have everyone set the app to stream content directly to G2 glasses.

title: Spotify Just Launched a New Running Mode, and I'm Surprised How Much I Love It
description: The kick drum got me to maintain every runner's dream: exactly 180bpm.
fullText:
I'm currently training for a marathon this fall, and today was supposed to be a rest day. Spotify had other plans for me: Today the company launched a new running mode, so I laced up and put it to the test.

This new mode cues up songs based on the different phases of your run and selects tracks based on your preferences and desired tempo. Instead of just shuffling a playlist and hoping the BPM lines up with your cadence, it builds a run around your effort structure: warmup, work intervals, recovery, cooldown. On top of the music, it layers in audio cues at key moments of the run, so you're getting something closer to a coached session, like Nike Run Club is known for.

Only paid subscribers can currently access this new running mode. Search "fitness" in the app to pull up what it calls the "Fitness Hub," and running mode is right at the top. From there, you can choose from one of 25 presets, or build your own from scratch.

Once you're in running mode, you first pick a workout type: Just Run, Easy Runs, Interval, Pyramid, or Long and Advanced. Then you choose a music genre. For me, the options were pop, hip-hop, EDM, rock, and R&B.

I messed around with a few presets before landing on the one I actually wanted to test properly: a Pyramid Rock Run. Here's how I "refined" it:

Bumped the duration from 30 to 35 minutes.

Workout type: I chose pyramid, which comes with a helpful graphic showing what the effort structure looks like over the course of the run.

More genre options showed up at this stage, including house, Latin, classical, and country. There's also a "discovery slider," so I pushed mine to 75% toward new music.

Toggled on using a target BPM for song selection, set it to 180, and also turned on "adjust song speed to match exactly," though after my test run, I'm not sure what this was supposed to do exactly.

After I locked in those settings, it took Spotify a solid two minutes to generate the playlist. Once it's built, you get options to smart reorder, add tracks, or refine further. Two things I noticed right away: It nailed the 75% new music request (fun!); the run started at 133 bpm (solid), climbed to a peak of 180 (perfect), and then the cooldown had one track sitting at 210 bpm (confusing and bad).

I thoroughly enjoyed my test run with this new feature today, even though I was supposed to be resting. Beyond the novelty, I think this is a genuinely good tool for runners trying to sharpen their internal sense of pace. Locking music tempo to target cadence gives you something to run alongside, and effort structures like pyramids force you to notice how your stride changes as intensity shifts. The audio coaching reminded me of what I've always liked about Nike Run Club: form cues and, more often than not, reminders to slow down, which is advice most runners need more than they know.

Spotify's AI coach delivers that guidance by way of music, always announcing each song, which I enjoyed. For instance, during the hip-hop playlist, one cue told me to "let the groove loosen my stride, and remember to unclench your fists and drop your shoulders." On the rock playlist, during a peak effort segment, it told me to "keep it snappy, but not forced." My pitch to Spotify here would be to announce the song's bpm, too.

One note worth remembering: the coach isn't actually responding to you in real time—it's all pre-set according to your workout preferences. Still, I approve of these built-in settings. The only real miss was that 210 bpm cooldown track. Everything else about the pacing logic tracked, which made that one outlier stand out more.

My favorite piece of coaching advice was to lock into the kick drum. I tried it during "Misery Business" by Paramore, and according to my Garmin Forerunner 970, I was running at exactly 180 bpm. Even if runners don't love the songs that Spotify selected for them (although I had no complaints personally), I'd still recommend this feature as a fun way to perfect your inner metronome and practice pacing before race day.

title: Here's What Lifehacker Readers Think Apple Will Announce in the Fall
description: These are the results of the second round of Lifehacker's Big Guessing Game.
fullText:
Lifehacker's Big Guessing Game finished its second round last week. The game invites readers to make predictions on what products and features Apple may announce this year, all for the chance to win the latest Apple Watch. While we won't know the answers of these questions until Apple's September event, we do have the results. Check out what Lifehacker readers think Apple will announce this year, and come back Aug. 18 to participate in the final round.

Apple is almost assuredly going to reveal its first foldable iPhone during WWDC this year. The major question left is, what will the company call it? Lifehacker asked readers to pick from the following four options: iPhone 18 Fold, iPhone Fold, iPhone Ultra, or none of the above. While iPhone Ultra was the most popular name choice, with 30% of readers choosing it, slightly more respondents think Apple will go with another name. We'll see who is right in just over a month.

Apple devices are notoriously expensive, and those prices are only continuing to rise. As such, it stands to reason that Apple's most complex and feature-filled iPhone yet will also be its priciest. Nearly a quarter of Lifehacker respondents believe the price will be somewhere between $1,000 and $1,499, while another near quarter think it'll cost $1,500 to $1,999. However, a whopping 41% believe it will cost more than $2,000. Personally, I think that's a good guess, considering the product and the current state of the market.

The iPhone 18 Pro will likely take a backseat to Apple's foldable iPhone, and, as such, will likely be a small upgrade over the iPhone 17 Pro. Still, rumors speculate that Apple will shrink the size of the Dynamic Island on the 18 Pro, to make it a bit less pronounced when looking at the display. A little less than 43% of respondents don't buy that, while just over 57% believe it. While it'd be great to get as close to no camera cutout as possible, for a truly screen-only iPhone front, I find the Dynamic Island useful, and I'm not sure making it smaller would improve that.

While the Apple Watch Series 11 can detect wrist temperature, Apple is also upgrading the health sensors on its wearables. As such, it's possible the next generation of Apple Waches could read your body temperature as a whole, replacing the need for dedicated thermometers. While nearly 18% don't think that's coming, over 82% do.

One AirPods rumor that has persisted for years is that Apple is working on embedding cameras in its earbuds. While that might sound ridiculous, the concept actually makes sense: Apple would use these cameras not to take pictures, but to allow Siri AI to see the world around you. It could turn your AirPods into an AI device, and eliminate the need for you to take out your iPhone every time you want to ask the assistant a visual question. That said, most Lifehacker readers don't think Apple will do this, including over 68% of respondents. We'll just have to see what Apple decides to do.

title: Study suggests the threat of mold-associated illnesses may be underappreciated
description: A first-of-its-kind U.S. study suggests invasive mold infections may be an underappreciated — and potentially deadly — threat.  The findings, published this week by the U.S.
fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — A first-of-its-kind U.S. study suggests invasive mold infections may be an underappreciated — and potentially deadly — threat.

The researchers detected about 450 cases in Atlanta-area hospitals over five years. About a third of the patients died in the hospital.

The findings, published this week by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, come from an attempt to better gauge how common these kinds of illnesses are. The government does not require doctors to report the illnesses.

"It's kind of the first time we've had an estimate like this," said the CDC's Dr. Jeremy Gold, the study's senior author.

And it's important to understand it now, because the problem may grow in the future, he added. Mold exposure is a recurring problem in the wake of hurricanes, floods and other natural disasters influenced by climate change, researchers have found.

"I agree that the frequency of fungal infections will likely increase with climate change," said Dr. Jeffrey Jenks, an infectious disease researcher at Duke University.

Meanwhile, there's a growing population of older people who are more susceptible to such illnesses, Gold said.

Invasive mold diseases are rare infections caused by certain species. Most people who get infected inhale mold spores, but they can also enter the body through cuts or wounds or from contaminated medical equipment.

The spores don't cause health problems for most people, but they can be life-threatening to some, including the elderly, cancer patients and others with weakened immune systems.

Previously, CDC researchers estimated more than 15,000 hospitalizations a year could be tied to invasive mold disease.

To better understand how common cases might be at a local level, the research team worked with four Atlanta-area hospitals and their affiliated outpatient clinics to look for potential cases from 2020 to 2024.

They initially identified nearly 1,000 potential cases, but winnowed the number down to about 450 by ruling out patients who may have had signs of exposure but didn't qualify as having invasive mold disease.

The researchers found that hospitals can expect to see 3 to 5 cases per year for every 100 inpatient beds. The rates were higher at larger academic hospitals that tend to see more complicated illnesses.

Most patients had impaired immune systems or — in a number of cases — were weakened after falling sick from COVID-19.

Mold exposures can occur in hospitals or other healthcare facilities, but the study did not try to determine where each patient was first exposed, Gold said.

It's hard to generalize what was seen in the Atlanta area to other parts of the country where mold may be more or less of a problem, he said. But it should give hospital administrators at least a rough idea about whether the number of cases they see is what might be expected or whether it's an outbreak, Gold added.

Jenks called the study's findings "valuable," but said "seeing results from similar studies done in different parts of the United States would be helpful."

title: Red state governor pummeled online after defying Trump’s deportation orders
description: Gov. Mike DeWine called Haiti "hell" while arguing against deporting Haitian TPS holders, sparking fierce online backlash from critics on social media.
fullText:
A Republican governor in a state that voted to elect President Donald Trump is facing intense backlash online after an interview arguing against the president's order to end Temporary Protected Status (TPS) migrants from the United States.

Republican Gov. Mike DeWine's state is home to an estimated 30,000 Haitian TPS holders. He told CBS earlier this week that the Haitians shouldn't be sent back to their country of origin.

"Haiti is hell today. So you'd be sending people… back to hell," he said. "Very few of these Haitians will voluntarily go back to Haiti. If they have to leave, they'll go someplace else. They want to work. They want to support their family. They don't want to go back to Haiti."

Blue State Leaders Erupt After Supreme Court's Decision Ending Tps Protections For Haitians, Syrians

Online detractors quickly seized on DeWine's comments, mostly from users claiming that those responsible for Haiti's conditions are the ones that the governor wants to allow to stay in the United States.

"What makes Haiti hellish? Is it… the Haitians?" asked Sean Davis, co-founder of The Federalist, in response to CBS' story about the interview posted on X.

"Hey governor, what is it that makes Haiti so bad anyway?" The Blaze's Logan Hall asked.

"I think the real question here is, if Haiti is hell, why are we importing Haitians?" questioned internet personality Larry Sanger.

Trump's 'Third World' Travel Ban Could Become Permanent If Firebrand Republican Lawmaker Gets Her Way

Others referenced the liberal media's freakout when, in 2018, Trump referred to Haiti and some other nations as "s---hole" countries.

Meanwhile, TV personalities and talking heads, comedian Conan O'Brien chief among them, defended Haiti for its natural beauty.

"Still reeling from [Trump's] very negative Yelp review of Haiti, which means I'll love it," O'Brien said at the time, announcing a trip to the country. "I have no idea what the president has against the people of Haiti, but if the president doesn't like them, they must be lovely people."

Dem-led Push To Extend Protections For Haitians Faces Outrage After Brutal Hammer Killing

One X user specifically blamed Haitians for DeWine's characterization that the country is "hell."

"Or is it a paradise like so many celebrities have said?" the user asked.

"I was reliably informed by democrats [sic] and hollywood [sic] celebrities that Haiti is utopia," said another user.

"What a tragedy it would be for Haitians to live in Haiti," said another X user.

DeWine argued in the CBS interview that sending Haitians back to Haiti would be a "mistake" that would endanger the lives of the TPS holders.

He also specifically mentioned Springfield, his hometown, which has a large population of Haitian TPS holders.

"These are people who have helped Springfield really come back," DeWine said. "The Haitians who are living there and employed there, they came there to work, and they came there because there were jobs that were not being filled by other people."

TPS was officially terminated Monday after Trump's order survived a Supreme Court review.

"Temporary Protected Status is exactly that — temporary. For too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent," a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson told Fox News Digital earlier this week.

TPS was created as part of the Immigration Act of 1990, and was designed for people facing serious emergencies like armed conflict or severe natural disasters. Critics claim it has been abused to give status to those in the U.S. for non-emergent reasons.

DeWine's office declined to comment on "statements made in online comment sections," when reached by Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment but did not hear back at time of publication.

Fox News Digital's Andrew Mark Miller contributed to this report.
