title: 'Nothing to prove' at Commonwealths for Finucane
description: Olympic team sprint champion Emma Finucane insists she has nothing to prove in Glasgow as she chases a Commonwealth gold medal.
fullText:
Olympic champion cyclist Emma Finucane insists she has "nothing to prove" at the Commonwealth Games despite her ambitions of winning an elusive gold in Scotland.

Finucane, 23, collected two bronze medals in Birmingham four years ago but has since won 16 medals at the Olympics, World and European Championships.

The Welsh star says she is targeting "the top step" on the podium in Glasgow.

"I haven't actually stood on the top step at the Commonwealth Games," Finucane told BBC Sport Wales.

"That's something I'd love to achieve this time round.

"I feel like I'm a different person four years on and I can't wait to show what I can do on the track."

The Carmarthenshire native credits the Birmingham 2022 Games as the "springboard" to where she is today.

"I would not be where I am today without the Commonwealth Games," she said.

"The first time I was pretty young, pretty naive to the sport of sprint cycling.

"It was a very overwhelming experience, whereas this time round I feel like I'm more of an established rider."

She added: "I was 19 [in Birmingham] and the year after I won my first world title, which was crazy for me.

"I think it gave me the confidence I needed as an athlete to develop in my career, and get to where I am so quickly.

"We became Olympic champions two years ago, and I actually don't even know how that happened."

Finucane will compete in the team sprint, the individual sprint, the 1km time trial and the keirin in Glasgow.

There is an impressive crop of British track cycling sprinters threatening her ambitions at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.

The England team has Finucane's Olympic gold-winning team-mates Sophie Capewell and Katy Marchant, while Rhianna Parris-Smith has helped Finucane to UCI Track World Cup silver in Hong Kong this year.

Scotland's Lauren Bell, who won sprint and keirin gold at the British Championships in 2024, could also provide stiff competition.

And that's before mentioning New Zealand's Ellesse Andrews, who won three golds in Birmingham in the individual sprint, keirin and team sprint competitions.

Wales at the Commonwealth Games

Finucane's partner, Matt Richardson is also a cyclist and represents England after switching allegiance from Australia.

She says they have a "fun relationship on the bike".

"We are really competitive people; if it's a game of Monopoly or it's a bike race, we are competitive and I think we use that to our strength.

Finucane says dating a fellow cyclist helps them to get what the other person might need, whether competitions have gone well or badly.

"He understands completely what I'm feeling or how the times are, what I'll be happy with or what I'll be disappointed with.

"That's something really nice and not many people get that.

"You can literally go to your partner and he'll be like 'It's okay'.

"He gives me so much advice on what I can do or how to deal with things and I'd like to say vice versa.

"He's a lot more experienced than me, but I think I do bring a presence of a bit more calm and maybe perspective in the sport too.

"I think we're a good team together."

Richardson however will no longer be competing at the Games after being forced out by injury.

Welsh rider Finucane sets new world sprint record

Finucane makes history with third medal in Paris

Finucane wants to be 'unstoppable' by 2028 Olympics

Finucane hopes a good showing in Glasgow will enhance her legacy in the sport.

"For us there's pressure everywhere, but I also feel calm coming into this Commonwealth Games; I have nothing to prove," she said.

"Obviously I do want to stand on that top step, and that will be the goal I'm trying to do; I've never achieved that in my career.

"But also I have my 'Oscars', as I call them.

"I won the Olympics, I've become world champion and I want to see how far I've gone in this sport.

"I want to win as much as I can, I want to be on the track as much as I can, representing Team Wales.

"So there is pressure. I'll definitely use that to drive me to try to win as many bike races as I can.

"It'll be insane to be in Glasgow, wearing the Welsh jersey, in front of my friends and family.

"I'm going to see how far I can go."

title: Scotland win eight medals in five chaotic hours as Games hit halfway
description: Host nation Scotland win eight medals in the space of five chaotic hours on Wednesday - two of them gold - to take their Commonwealth Games tally in Glasgow to 23.
fullText:
Host nation Scotland won eight medals in the space of five chaotic hours on Wednesday - two of them gold - to take their Commonwealth Games tally in Glasgow to 23.

Swimmers Angharad Evans and Keanna MacInnes both won an individual medal and a relay prize, and Toni Shaw also tasted success in the pool at Tollcross.

Melanie Woods roared to gold on the track at Scotstoun, before Steven MacKenzie earned a surprise bronze in the field.

And at the SEC, both the men's 3x3 basketball team and their women's wheelchair equivalents ended the evening on the podium.

It takes Scotland's tally to 23 overall as the Games passes the halfway mark - nine gold and seven of both silver and bronze.

And it is the best return in a single day since nine were claimed on the last day of the Birmingham edition in 2022.

Woods sets Games record to claim gold for Scotland

No car park tears this time for Love as 3x3 teams claim silver & bronze

After a relatively quiet day, the first medal was claimed by the men's 3x3 basketball team just before 17:00 BST.

A couple of hours later, three more followed in the space of five minutes.

The women's wheelchair 3x3 basketball team took silver; Evans added her second gold - and third medal - of the Games in the 200m breaststroke; then Woods claimed gold in the women's T54 1500m.

Shaw then joined in with bronze in the women's S9 100m freestyle before MacInnes was edged into second place in the women's 200m butterfly to take her second individual silver of the meet.

Around the same time, MacKenzie was leaping to long jump bronze, before the haul was completed in the pool when Evans and MacInnes teamed up with Katie Shanahan and Evie Davis to take silver in the women's 4x100m medley.

Three more further medals are guaranteed in boxing - with fighters in semi-final action on Friday - while further prospects remain in athletics, bowls, cycling, judo and weightlifting.

title: No car park tears this time for Love as 3x3 teams claim silver & bronze
description: After tears in Birmingham four years ago, Robyn Love gets on to the podium at the Commonwealth Games.
fullText:
Four years ago, in a converted car park in Birmingham, tears fell down Robyn Love's cheeks and thumping music assaulted her ears.

A Commonwealth Games that started with a lost chair had ended in a missed opportunity for Scotland's women's wheelchair 3x3 basketball team.

A bronze medal had been lost to hosts England amid the rambunctious surroundings of Smithfield Market, and Love was trying to explain how much it hurt when her emotions took over.

Fast forward four years and the 35-year-old from Ayr was the sole survivor from that team as Scotland faced England again on Wednesday in Glasgow.

The difference this time was that it was in the gold-medal match.

Love, Lea Smith, Kayli English and Jodie Waite knew they would leave the SEC with - at worst - a slab of silver around their necks after beating Australia in the semi-final earlier in the day. And ultimately that's what happened after an 18-10 defeat.

That they - officially at least - missed out on becoming Scotland's first ever Commonwealth medallists in a team sport after being usurped by their men's 3x3 pals winning bronze earlier in the day will not have concerned them in the slightest.

"I'm not crying now, but I pretty much was this morning after the semi-final," said veteran Love, who also coaches this callow team.

"To get a Commonwealth silver with this group, and to get to coach them and see them grow... what a privilege. I feel incredibly lucky and it's much better being in the SEC than in a car park in Birmingham, I can tell you that for free."

Kerr and Wightman revel in Wednesday warm-up for mile final

The 23-year-old teacher leading lesson on stripping bowls' stigma

All the latest from Team Scotland at the Games

Two of the men's team are no strangers to Games pain either.

Kyle Jimenez and Ross Malcolm lost in the bronze-medal game to New Zealand in Gold Coast in 2018, and again four years later against Canada.

They were not going to let their opportunity pass a third time.

New Zealand - who had beaten them in the round robin - were the opposition again, but the Scottish-born duo - and US-raised team-mates Skylar White and Owen McCormack - kept their shape in an angst-ridden contest to win 18-16.

"We needed to keep it interesting for you guys," White, whose father is from Kilmarnock, told fans afterwards.

He added: "Towards the end, I told the guys 'you can be hurt tomorrow, you can feel sore tomorrow, but right now it's time to nut up and get it done'."

McCormack, who qualifies through his Scottish mother, said the feeling of taking bronze ranked among the "top two... and it's not two" in his life.

He also paid tribute to Malcolm and Jimenez, who have long been passionate advocates for the sport in Scotland as well as elite performers.

And that duo spoke movingly about what this success could mean in a wider sense.

"Coming into this we all believed we could get a medal as a team, but no one else thought anything of us - we proved the world wrong today," Jimenez said.

Malcolm added: "Every time we play on an international stage we punch above our weight. Hopefully we get the coverage and the publicity that the sport deserves."

Amid the joy, though, there was disappointment for the wheelchair men's team, who lost their bronze-medal match to Canada 19-9.

title: From bad to worse for Trump and his base
description: Republicans are starting to fret about their base’s lack of enthusiasm ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
fullText:
Republicans are starting to fret about their base's lack of enthusiasm ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

Those voters were already disproportionately less likely to vote in elections not featuring Donald Trump, and now the GOP has to contend with the president being more unpopular than ever.

And a new CNN poll drives home the problem: Large portions of Trump's base are feeling disillusioned over more than a few of his choices lately.

Across a bevy of questions — on subjects ranging from the economy to the Iran war to Trump's self-enrichment and efforts to makeover Washington — large percentages of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents are registering discontent. As in, often 30%, 40%, 50% or more.

Overall, the CNN poll shows 30% of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents disapprove of Trump.

That number is rather high in and of itself. But it actually might undersell the level of disillusionment on some fronts.

Without question, the most troubling numbers for Trump and the GOP concern the economy.

Not only is the economy generally voters' biggest concern; it also features Trump's worst numbers.

To wit, among Republicans and GOP-leaning independents in the poll:

64% say high gas prices have caused at least a "moderate" hardship for them

56% say the economy is very or somewhat poor

56% say Trump hasn't gone far enough to reduce the price of everyday goods

56% disapprove of Trump's performance on gas prices

51% say Trump doesn't have a clear plan on gas prices

50% say Trump's policies haven't improved economic conditions (with 31% saying his policies have actually made things worse)

47% disapprove of Trump on inflation

That's around half or more of what should be Trump's own supporters that have a lot of gripes about the economy and his handling of it right now.

The numbers are slightly less grim on Iran, but still pretty grim.

Again, among Republicans and GOP-leaning independents:

64% think a long-term war with Iran is likely

45% say the toll of the war — in lives and money — hasn't been worth it

45% say Trump doesn't have a clear plan for Iran

40% disapprove of Trump overall on Iran

39% say his decisions about military action in Iran have hurt the US (versus 44% who say it has helped, with the rest being neutral)

And Trump's trend line on Iran continues to be bad. Trump's disapproval on Iran among these groups has increased from 30% in March to 40% today.

The poll also shows many members of Trump's base simply don't like what he's focused on — including his personal finances and projects like the White House ballroom and Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

45% say Trump isn't "in touch with the problems ordinary Americans face in their daily lives" — up from 34% in January

39% say he hasn't paid enough attention to the country's most important problems — up from 25% in January

Around 3 in 10 say he's "gone too far" in changing institutions like the Smithsonian and the Kennedy Center (which Trump put his name on before a judge removed it), remodeling the White House and other Washington landmarks and pursuing personal business interests while in the White House

30% say Trump doesn't put the good of the country over his personal gain

26% say they're angry or dissatisfied about the ballroom and the reflecting pool (compared to just 39% who are positive about these projects)

It would be bad enough for Trump if the economy were suboptimal and people didn't think the things he did were working.

But these numbers — combined with the majority of Trump's base that says he's neglected inflation — make clear many of his backers think he's preoccupied with things that either aren't worth focusing on or are actively unpopular.

When many of these questions were asked in Trump's first months back in office, there was a palpable sense of enthusiasm with his base.

When asked to describe their feelings looking ahead to the rest of Trump's second term, nearly nine in 10 of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents said they were "enthusiastic" or "optimistic."

Now, that number has dropped all the way to 70%.

And 30% say they're either "pessimistic" or "afraid."

That 30% who have a negative outlook is pretty remarkable. Shortly after former President Barack Obama was reelected in 2012, just 8% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents said they felt pessimistic or afraid. And just before former President George W. Bush's reelection in 2004, only 5% of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents said the same about him.

Then there's the findings of a recent Pew Research Center poll.

That poll showed 81% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents said their midterm vote would be a vote against Trump, compared to just 44% of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents who said theirs would be a vote for Trump.

There have been signs of this kind of malaise dating back a year, when the Jeffrey Epstein saga exploded. The latest numbers suggest it's now taken hold in large swaths of the GOP base — at a very inopportune time for the party.

title: Laura Ingraham stands at Fauci hearing alongside others ‘shamed’ during COVID-19
description: Fox News host Laura Ingraham was on hand to watch Dr. Anthony Fauci answer questions at Wednesday’s Senate hearing, sitting behind him and standing up when Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) asked about peop...
fullText:
Fox News host Laura Ingraham was on hand to watch Dr. Anthony Fauci answer questions at Wednesday's Senate hearing, sitting behind him and standing up when Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) asked about people being "shamed" during the COVID-19 pandemic.

When Moreno requested people in the audience stand up if they had controversial beliefs or actions surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic and may have faced backlash for those beliefs or actions, Ingraham stood.

"All you have to do is look up from your lawyers and look at the people who were absolutely shamed for saying what we know now to be the truth," Moreno told Fauci during the hearing.

Ingraham, as the COVID-19 pandemic was raging in the U.S., criticized the use of coronavirus vaccines and said that Americans should not have to receive them.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, conservatives often raged against public health measures and advice meant to protect against the virus, including masking and vaccinations.

Fauci, the former chief White House medical adviser, invoked his Fifth Amendment right at a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on Wednesday held by the committee's chair, Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.).

Fauci went after Paul's "obvious obsession" with calling for the health official's prosecution. Fauci and Paul have a history of tension during congressional hearings.

"The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something, anything that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, 'behind bars,'" Fauci said.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Resurfaced video shows James Talarico discussing ‘exciting’ opportunity to end ‘over-policing’
description: Resurfaced video shows James Talarico calling efforts to end over-policing "really exciting" after 2020 Black Lives Matter riots in Austin, Texas.
fullText:
EXCLUSIVE: A resurfaced video shows that following the 2020 Black Lives Matter riots in the wake of George Floyd's death, now-Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico said the country was facing a "really exciting" opportunity to "end the current situation of over-policing communities of color which has been in place in this country since its founding."

Talarico, a Texas state lawmaker, is tied in recent polling with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the race to be the state's next U.S. senator. Such a flip would be the first in decades and would deal a major blow to the GOP's chances of retaining a Senate majority. Despite a history of controversial statements, including calling God nonbinary and claiming there are six genders, Talarico has recently positioned himself as a moderate, pro-police candidate.

However, critics are calling his pro-police stance into question after they say the resurfaced video destroys that narrative.

Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, ripped Talarico as a "dangerous freak who is willing to endanger the entire state just to prove that he is sufficiently woke."

Far-left Senate Hopeful Explains 'Ogre On A Pike' Remark After Getting Torched By His Own Party

Kraft alleged that "James Talarico's wacked out vision for Texas with no police, no prisons, and no borders would put families in danger and be a paradise for criminal illegal aliens."

Unearthed clips from a September 2020 Zoom with South Asian American Voter Empowerment (SAAVETX) show Talarico saying that policymakers need to "listen to black voices and to the activists in the streets calling for a radically different vision of public safety."

He ripped Republicans who he accused of wanting to "scare white people to win an election," saying that "is a time-honored tradition in the Republican Party."

Talarico asserted that "police violence against communities of color, in particular our black community is nothing new, and has its roots in slavery and Jim Crow and mass incarceration."

He added that "this is just the latest iteration of the history of oppression this country has been a part of against African Americans."

Meanwhile, he said he would like to gather people "from activists and advocates to community leaders to law enforcement officials themselves to have a genuine discussion about what true public safety policy looks like and how we can end the current situation of over-policing communities of color which has been in place in this country since its founding."

He added that the discussion should be about "how do we take our criminal justice system at the state level, at the national level, and how do we make some fundamental changes to reflect our highest ideals and to really embody the country and state and the community that we want in the race to be."

"That's taking place," he continued, adding that communities are "figuring out how we reinvest our limited public funding into these community-based solutions that really start to address the underlying causes of our criminal justice system attempts to treat."

"That to me is really exciting," he said.

Talarico proceeded to say, "I applaud our local leaders that are trying to do that." He cited the city of Austin, which had recently approved a budget that cut tens of millions of dollars from the Austin Police Department. He ripped Republican Gov. Greg Abbott for having "proposed removing some of the revenue streams from cities like Austin because they've made local decisions for their local community."

At the time, Abbott released a statement saying that "Austin's decision puts the brave men and women of the Austin Police Department and their families at greater risk, and paves the way for lawlessness." The governor promised financial penalties for any Texas city defunding its police force, saying, "Public safety is job one, and Austin has abandoned that duty."

During the Zoom call, however, Talarico asserted that for Abbott to "complain about local communities not funding public safety is hypocritical."

"To see the governor continue to try to undermine our local governments, I think is rich to say the least," he said.

In response to the new criticism, JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico's campaign, told Fox News Digital that "James opposes defunding the police, has voted to deny bail for violent criminals, and has a record of sending billions of dollars to support law enforcement."

Additionally, Ennis said that Talarico "supports a secure southern border and has unveiled a border security agenda backed by law enforcement officials from both parties."

Meanwhile, he accused Paxton of having "abused his office to benefit his wealthy donors and the well-connected, allowing criminals back on the street even as it made Texans less safe," adding, "Even Ken Paxton's fellow Republicans have blasted his public safety record: more murders, soft on human trafficking, and pedophiles walking free."

Ennis has previously called the assertion that Talarico is pro-defund the police a "flat out lie."

He said that previous legislation proposed by Talarico "supports the police by adding desperately needed mental health officials to help prevent tragic events like the mass shooting at Robb Elementary in Uvalde, Texas."

Madison Cercy, a spokesperson for Paxton's campaign, said that "James Talarico has the most consistently anti-law enforcement record in the Texas Legislature. But now his spokesman is out telling bold-faced lies."

"For his campaign to even insinuate that Talarico has, at any point in his career, 'stood with law enforcement' is one of the most egregious lies they have told throughout this campaign," Cercy told Fox News Digital.

She said that Talarico "donated thousands of dollars to an organization that supported defunding the police and voted against banning personal bond release for people accused of violent crimes," while emphasizing that "just because he votes on a basic spending bill like every other state representative does not mean he has ever 'supported law enforcement.'"

"If it were up to Talarico," she continued, "We would hand over our communities to the radicals who pillaged our streets during the 2020 defund the police movement and let criminals out of prison in pursuit of a socialist agenda."

title: Pretorius drives Spirit to win over MI London
description: Lhuan-dre Pretorius recovers from a heavy collision in the field to hit 64 as London Spirit beat MI London by seven wickets for their first win in this season's Hundred.
fullText:
The Hundred men's competition, The Oval

MI London 164-5 (100 balls): Jacks 65 (44); Overton 3-30

London Spirit 165-3 (89 balls): Pretorius 64 (28); Gleeson 1-23

London Spirit won by seven wickets

Lhuan-dre Pretorius recovered from a heavy collision in the field to hit 64 as London Spirit beat MI London by seven wickets for their first win in this season's Hundred.

The South African and James Coles ran into one another chasing a catch late in the first innings, in which reach MI London reached 164-5.

Pretorius left the field after the incident but was fit to open the Spirit innings and hit three fours and seven sixes in his 28-ball innings, which started with a 63-run partnership with Jonny Bairstow (23).

The 20-year-old added a further 38 with Liam Livingstone (16) before he was caught by Sherfane Rutherford off the bowling of Richard Gleeson.

James Rew (19) and Dewald Brevis (37 from 18) finished the job off for Spirit, who won with 11 balls to spare.

MI London had started well after being put into bat, with Will Jacks (65) and James Vince (26) putting on a 91-run opening partnership.

However both openers and Nicholas Pooran fell in the space of eight balls as the home side slipped to 100-3.

Both Jacks and Pooran were dismissed by Jamie Overton, who later removed Jason Roy (13) for figures of 3-30.

Rutherford accelerated at the close for MI, striking a 19-ball 41 that featured four sixes before he was caught by Coles off Andrew Tye from the last ball of the innings.

Spirit move into sixth, above Southern Brave and Birmingham Phoenix, after claiming their first win in three matches, while MI London sit in fourth with two wins and two defeats.

In the women's competition, the home side, who sit at the top of the table, will be aiming for a fourth win from as many matches, while Phoenix are yet to win after two games. They meet at 15:00 BST.

title: Evans battles nerves to become Scotland's breakout star
description: Angharad Evans added another breaststroke gold to become Scotland's breakout star in the pool at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
fullText:
Angharad Evans describes herself as a "nervous swimmer" who dare not even let herself think of getting a medal. She ended the Commonwealth Games swimming meet as Scotland's breakout star.

Double breaststroke gold, and a relay bronze and silver means her strategy of keeping expectations low must work. But after an imperious performance across the week at a raucous Tollcross, they will never be as low again.

After recovering from a slow start, Evans powered to 200m breaststroke gold to add to her first place in the 100m on the final night of swimming action, during which Scotland claimed four medals.

A couple of hours later Evans' superb second leg helped Scotland into silver medal position behind Australia in the women's 4x100m medley relay - her fourth medal of these home games.

Only one of her training partners at Stirling University, Duncan Scott no less, tipped her for big things in Glasgow. Even Evans did not believe.

"It's been a big step forward in my career," Evans told BBC Scotland.

"There are things I've battled with this week. I don't hide from my nerves - it's something I'm very open about.

"I'm a very nervous swimmer but I proved to myself that even though I am nervous I can get medals individually and in relays, even when I'm tired on the last day.

"But it makes it a lot easier doing in front of a crowd like that and with your team-mates you train with every day."

Scotland win eight medals in five chaotic hours as Games hit halfway

Woods sets Games record to claim gold for Scotland

Kerr and Wightman revel in Wednesday warm-up for mile final

Evans, like many of her team-mates, has memories to cherish from these Glasgow Games. After her 200m gold she looked almost stunned as the crowd went nuts around her.

Evans emerged from the water and tried to take it all in. Her family and boyfriend were scattered around the small arena, but she managed to spot them all and get hugs. There was even a guard of honour with team-mates bedecked in kilts.

It was all so far from what Evans had allowed herself to dream of.

"I disassociate the idea of getting a medal because that's when I operate best," the Cambridge-born athlete said.

"It was a very special moment for me. Going into the Commonwealth Games with no expectations and coming out with two gold medals and a bronze [and silver] in the relay has just been so surreal.

"It just shows the hard work that we've been doing in Stirling."

So, can this be the springboard for more?

"Right now it's just taking a breath and taking it in before we hit Europeans [Championships next week]. We'll see what happens there.

"But as I said, I think this is a really big step forward for me - and hopefully the Europeans will be another step forward. I won't go out without a fight."

Evans steps out of shadows into spotlight with Scotland's fourth gold

A Scottish gold made up for the fact Scott missed out on his bid to defend his 200m freestyle title and add a 16th Commonwealth medal, having failed to qualify for the final at the end of a rigorous schedule.

And Evans' success was not the only one cheered to the roof of Tollcross instead.

Aberdeen's Toni Shaw stopped an Australian clean sweep of medals in the women's S9 100m freestlye final to replicate the bronze of Birmingham four years ago.

"I had lots and lots of nerves even before the walkout, all day since my heat," Shaw told BBC Scotland.

"But we've got a good support team and they helped me keep my cool and wish me luck. All you can do is swim as fast as you can and that's the mentality I went into the race with."

Meanwhile, Keanna MacInnes added 200m butterfly silver, having also come second in the 100m. The 24-year-old played her part in the relay silver too to take her own tally to three.

As she stood next to her relay team-mates Katie Shanahan, Evans, and Evelyn Davis the Stirling swimmer reflected on a Games during which Scottish swimmers have delivered 12 medals, four of them gold.

"If you said to me at the start of the week I'd win two medals I'd be over the moon - sneaking that extra mixed medley one last night was special for all of us," MacInnes said.

"We heard it a 100 times, about the crowd being amazing but it absolutely delivered. I'm a proud and patriotic Scot so there's been a lot of tears this week.

"Not only is it 12 medals but there are a lot of golds and silvers, not necessarily sneaking into bronze. That shows the depth.

"There were so many finals with multiple Scots in them. So not just medals but lots of personal and season's bests which shows how good the team has been this week."

title: 'Change is inevitable' - Liverpool CEO on FSG, Iraola and consortium talks
description: Liverpool Billy Hogan talks to BBC Sport in New York about investment, transition and why FSG aren't done yet.
fullText:
With Liverpool stating that they have more than 26 million supporters in the USA, there is little surprise over why the Reds chose America as the destination for their pre-season tour.

This has been quite the summer for football here and Billy Hogan, CEO of Liverpool and Fenway Sports Group (FSG), insists the aim is to build on that after what has been a "super difficult year" for the club "for lots of different reasons."

Hogan is speaking to BBC Sport in New York ahead of Andoni Iraola's side taking on Wrexham at the famous Yankee Stadium on Wednesday evening at 19:30 local time, 00:30 BST.

However, for all the excitement around a new era on the pitch, it is events off the pitch that must be addressed first.

Last week, FSG, which owns Liverpool, confirmed that a consortium led by Amit Bhatia, a British-Indian millionaire businessman, was in talks over a strategic minority investment in the club. Those talks have been ongoing and there is a growing belief that a deal will be done.

"Look, John Henry (the principal owner) and FSG have always said that if there was an interest in an investment that would help the football club, then they would consider it. That was said many years ago and that remains the case here," Hogan tells BBC Sport.

"At this point, I wouldn't say anything different to the statement that a consortium led, managed and represented by Amit Bhatia has come forward and expressed an interest in a minority investment."

Hogan, who has been with FSG since they purchased Liverpool for £300m in 2010, does stress though that they are still very much committed to the project and that news of this development should not be seen as a sign of the company, which also owns the Major League Baseball franchise, Boston Red Sox, stepping away.

According to the Financial Times, a deal with the consortium led by Bhatia would value Liverpool at more than £4.5bn.

"There's a huge opportunity still," Hogan says. "This is the biggest and most popular sport in the world and we're one of the biggest clubs in the biggest league in the biggest sport in the world. So that's a great place for us to be. The Premier League has a tremendous amount of momentum behind it.

"We've definitely not peaked. We're in a good place to continue to grow and that's why everyone across both sides of the club, football and business and whether they kick a ball or not, is focused on driving the club forward and winning trophies.

"On the pitch, our goal every season is to win trophies. Off the pitch, our priority is to continue driving overall revenues and expand and build the club.

"We're really happy with the trajectory and direction of the club - we were fifth in the Deloitte Football Money League and had the highest revenue (£702m) in the Premier League.

"All of that investment, as has always been the case since 2010, goes back into the club. It's about running the club sustainably."

Who is potential investor Bhatia?

Consortium in talks to buy Liverpool minority stake

After a record summer spend last season of £450m, Liverpool were disappointing on the pitch.

Ultimately, that led to the sacking of Arne Slot at the end of the campaign. Senior players like Mohamed Salah, Andy Robertson and Ibrahima Konate all left on free transfers too.

It has been a summer of change at Liverpool with Michael Edwards stepping down as FSG's CEO of football, primarily because plans of multi-club ownership were abandoned.

Meanwhile, Richard Hughes, Liverpool's sporting director, is linked with a move to Al Hilal in Saudi Arabia. There is certainly a question of stability.

"Transition and change is inevitable in football. In our case, with a new coach coming in, there's real excitement around Andoni's mindset and philosophy that supporters will really enjoy," says Hogan.

"That will take time but in terms of transition, I would send a message that we are in a very healthy place as a football club - the leadership from ownership is in a very steady place and we're looking forward to the next season and the season ahead."

Hogan insists that regardless of the personnel changes, the club model remains the same and they will continue to stick to their principles.

"It's important to keep in mind that last season, a considerable amount was invested but also generated in terms of sales of players going out," he says. "Over the course of FSG's stewardship, the investment has always been focused on doing what's best to put us in a place to win.

"Sometimes that means significant expense and other times it doesn't like in the summer of 2024 when there was only one addition (Federico Chiesa for £12.5m). It depends on where we are at the club and the improvements needed. Ultimately Mike Gordon, who is really our managing owner, will make those decisions."

There is an increased focus on the women's team too, who finished 11th in the WSL last season and haven't won the top-flight title since 2014.

"To be self-critical, that is probably an area that we maybe took our eye off the ball several years ago but we've changed that," says Hogan.

"We now have one of the best training centres at AXA Melwood, we are investing in the squad and we will approach the women's team the same way we approach the men's team - which is to run it sustainably. There's tremendous growth in the women's game and a huge opportunity going forward to really drive that."

Liverpool preparing opening bid for PSG's Barcola

It is still remarkable to think now that the club was on the verge of administration when FSG took over in 2010.

It hasn't all been plain sailing. As recently as this year, Hogan wrote to fans over ticket price increases. The club cut the size of their planned rise in ticket prices for the next couple of seasons after fan protests.

However, under FSG's stewardship, Anfield has been transformed, with two of the four stands developed in the last decade.

"Back when FSG acquired LFC, a number of similarities were drawn with Boston Red Sox and Liverpool and one of them was this idea of an iconic venue that truly sits in the community," says Hogan. "One of the things we're focused on now is making improvements in the footprint around Anfield the neighbourhood whether that's infrastructure or transport and getting people in on non-match days. We're proud of how we've expanded while keeping the soul but also modernising it in the way that's befitting of the football club.

"Football doesn't give you much time to sit back and reflect. What I would say I am most proud of is that the club is in such a positive and good financial position. If you go back to that point in 2010, the club was literally on the brink of bankruptcy. Now it has the right foundations underneath it. There's improvements across the infrastructure, the ability to stay at Anfield for the long-term and the stuff that doesn't always get headlines but are super important for the health of the club.

"Ultimately, it's about winning trophies and I wish we could win more but we've been fortunate to win a few.

"I think our supporters have had a great time and I often think about the fan parks at the Champions League finals - we lost a couple but just that joy and the memories and frankly the fun of it is what I look back from time to time. And it's something that everyone associated with Liverpool should be proud of because it happens together and we all want this club to be the best in the world."

After a torrid year for Liverpool, where better to start looking ahead than in New York, the city of dreams?

title: Boxer Abdul - grandson of dictator - disqualified for headbutt
description: Ugandan boxer Aziz Abdul - the grandson of dictator Idi Amin - was disqualified from his fight at the Commonwealth Games after appearing to headbutt his English opponent.
fullText:
Ugandan boxer Aziz Abdul - the grandson of dictator Idi Amin - was disqualified from his fight at the Commonwealth Games after appearing to headbutt his English opponent.

The 25-year-old was punished after lifting his head into Damar Thomas' chin as the pair grappled in the third round.

Abdul later claimed the judges were against him because he is a "black African".

"When you watch the previous fights of England their boxers create a lot of fouls," he said.

"I land a heavy punch on him, they never count. Instead of counting they deduct me.

"I am black African. He is in homeland."

Idi Amin's boxer grandson determined to become new King of Scotland

Before the super-heavyweight bout Abdul told the BBC he wanted to become the new 'King of Scotland' - in reference to Amin declaring himself that name in 1976.

After taking power in a coup in 1971, Amin ran a brutal regime during which an estimated half a million people were killed. He was also known as the Butcher of Uganda.

Abdul, who never met his grandfather, was chasing Uganda's first Commonwealth boxing medal since Auckland in 1990 - something which would have been guaranteed had he beaten Thomas.

Instead, he was given warnings in the previous two rounds and was trailing on all of the judges' scorecards.

"All I can say about this is the decision is not right, I am not happy," he said.

"He elbowed me. He caught me with the elbow.

"It [the head movement] was not intentional. I was trying to come back.

"How can I headbutt someone? I would not.

"He was the person they wanted to win. He was the winner before.

"I knew if I did not get knockout I could not win the fight."

BBC Sport has contacted Commonwealth Games organisers and World Boxing for a response to Abdul's comments.

Thomas, who is now guaranteed at least a bronze medal, said it was "not the way" he wanted to win.

"I can't change what happened today but I can control how I box on Friday," he said.

Amin, himself a boxer, harboured a fascination with Scotland after serving in the King's African Rifles in his 20s.

At the height of the regime, he was fond of wearing a kilt and playing the bagpipes - and even declared himself "King of Scotland" in 1976.

Some years later, those predilections even spawned an Oscar-winning film, The Last King of Scotland, starring Forest Whitaker and James McAvoy.

In a previous interview, Abdul said he was "inspired" by Amin, although it was not entirely clear whether he was talking about his boxing feats or not.

Speaking to the BBC, he refused to answer when asked if he was proud to be the dictator's grandson, but he did address the question of how he feels when he is linked to someone with such a sinister reputation.

title: Lloyd pays tribute to 'greatest' Sobers at funeral
description: Sir Garfield Sobers is called the "greatest all-round cricketer the world has ever known" by former team-mate Sir Clive Lloyd at the legendary West Indies player's state funeral in Barbados.
fullText:
Sir Garfield Sobers was called the "greatest all-round cricketer the world has ever known" by former team-mate Sir Clive Lloyd at the legendary West Indies player's state funeral in Barbados.

Lloyd described all-rounder Sobers, who died aged 89 on 17 July, as "a man who lived in the hearts and minds of Caribbean people and who became a source of inspiration to millions throughout the world".

An entertaining left-handed batter and bowler of seam and spin, Sobers played 93 Tests between 1954 and 1974, scoring 8,032 runs and taking 235 wickets.

The funeral was staged at the Kensington Oval in Bridgetown, the principle ground in Barbados and home to a pavilion named after Sobers.

Lloyd and fellow West Indies legends Brian Lara and Desmond Haynes were among those who spoke at the state service of thanksgiving, which was also attended by Barbados president Jeffrey Bostic, prime minister Mia Mottley and Barbadian music superstar Rihanna.

West Indies Test captain Roston Chase, who comes from Barbados, vice-captain Jomel Warrican and the current side's Barbadian players were also in attendance, having completed a Test victory over Pakistan on Monday, winning by 90 runs inside four days in Trinidad.

"Sir Garfield Sobers was not merely the outstanding cricketer of his generation," Lloyd added. "He brought to the beautiful game a rare combination of brilliance, imagination, courage and joy."

Sobers' coffin was draped in the flag of Barbados and set off from the Parliament Buildings in Bridgetown on a gun carriage for a formal procession through the nation's capital.

On arrival at the stadium, the carriage passed through a guard of honour of raised cricket bats.

"This is not a sad moment," Lara said of his mentor. "This is a moment for us to celebrate and I hope you feel the same. Today we celebrate the remarkable life of the greatest all-round cricketer.

"We celebrate a man who gave so much to his family, to Barbados, to the West Indies and all of us who had the privilege of knowing him."

Sobers scored 365 not out against Pakistan in 1958 - an effort which stood as the record Test score for 36 years.

He was also named one of Wisden's five cricketers of the 20th century.

During his stint at Nottinghamshire in 1968, Sobers became the first player to hit a six off all six balls in an over in a first-class match.

Mottley described Sobers as "a man who if he had not achieved any of those great feats on the cricket field would have been immortalised by his community as a good man and a great man".

Reverend Canon Guy Hewitt read out a message from King Charles during the service.

"History is distinguished with sporting champions whose records have rightly commanded respect across generations," the message read. "There have been far fewer however whose name along brings a smile to people's faces across Barbados, the Caribbean and the Commonwealth.

"Sir Garfield Sobers belongs very firmly in the latter category. I send my deepest sympathies to Sir Garry's family as they come to terms with this great loss."

Sobers' body lay in state at the Barbados parliament on Monday and at the Kensington Oval on Tuesday, with national dignitaries and members of the public able to pay their respects.

He will be laid to rest at Coral Ridge Memorial Gardens in the south of Barbados.
